## Research question
Is Sablewing a more efficient sampler than Ordell-DDS for 256×256 face generation, and what does it cost in sample quality?

## Methods summary
Sablewing distils the Ordell-DDS denoiser into a student network that generates an image in 8 denoising steps (8 network function evaluations, NFE). The student is slightly wider than the teacher, so each of its evaluations costs somewhat more compute. Ordell-DDS is the 50-step teacher sampler; Ordell-DDS-10 runs the same sampler truncated to 10 steps.

## Experimental setup
Each sampler generates 30,000 images at 256×256 resolution for Halvern-Faces; FID is computed against the full Halvern-Faces reference set (lower is better). NFE counts denoiser evaluations per image, and TFLOPs per image are computed analytically from the network architecture and NFE. All models use fp16 weights.

## Experiments and comparisons
- `exp1`: Sampler comparison on Halvern-Faces 256×256
  - comparison `exp1/cmp1`: Sablewing vs Ordell-DDS (50 steps): sampling cost and FID
  - comparison `exp1/cmp2`: Sablewing vs Ordell-DDS-10: sampling cost and FID

## Results tables

sentences.text: On Halvern-Faces at 256×256 resolution, Sablewing reduces sampling cost by 6.25× in NFE (8 vs. 50) and 5.7× in TFLOPs per image (0.94 vs. 5.40) relative to the 50-step Ordell-DDS teacher, at the cost of a higher FID (7.8 vs. 7.1).

Compared with the 10-step truncated Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing is slightly cheaper in TFLOPs (0.94 vs. 1.08) and substantially better in FID (7.8 vs. 15.6), despite using fewer denoising steps (8 vs. 10).
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in FID and cost are descriptive only and cannot be claimed as significant.

On Halvern-Faces at 256×256 resolution, Sablewing reduces sampling cost by 5.7× in NFE (8 vs. 50) and 5.7× in TFLOPs per image (0.94 vs. 5.40) relative to the 50-step Ordell-DDS teacher, at the cost of a higher FID (7.8 vs. 7.1).

Compared with the 10-step truncated Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing is slightly cheaper in TFLOPs (0.94 vs. 1.08) and substantially better in FID (7.8 vs. 15.6), despite using fewer denoising steps (8 vs. 10).
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in FID and cost are descriptive only and cannot be claimed as significant.
On Halvern-Faces at 256×256 resolution, Sablewing uses 8 NFE and 0.94 TFLOPs per image versus 50 NFE and 5.40 TFLOPs for the 50-step Ordell-DDS teacher, while achieving a higher FID (7.8 vs. 7.1).
Compared with the 10-step truncated Ordell-DDS-10, Sablewing uses fewer denoising steps (8 vs. 10) and lower TFLOPs (0.94 vs. 1.08), with a lower FID (7.8 vs. 15.6).
No statistical tests were reported, so these differences are descriptive and limited to the single dataset and resolution evaluated.

On Halvern-Faces 256×256, Sablewing is substantially more efficient than the 50-step Ordell-DDS teacher, requiring 0.94 TFLOPs per image and 8 NFE versus 5.40 TFLOPs and 50 NFE, at the cost of a higher FID (7.8 vs 7.1).
Compared with the 10-step truncated teacher (Ordell-DDS-10), Sablewing is both more efficient (0.94 vs 1.08 TFLOPs; 8 vs 10 NFE) and achieves a lower FID (7.8 vs 15.6).

Thus, Sablewing's sample quality is worse than the full 50-step teacher but better than the 10-step truncated baseline, indicating a quality cost relative to the full teacher and a quality gain over the truncated baseline; no statistical tests were reported, so these FID differences are descriptive only.
